question:
A unit cube has vertices \(P_1,\) \(P_2,\) \(P_3,\) \(P_4,\) \(P_1',\) \(P_2',\) \(P_3',\) and \(P_4'.\) Vertices \(P_2,\) \(P_3,\) and \(P_4\) are adjacent to \(P_1,\) and for \(1 \le i \le 4,\) vertices \(P_i\) and \(P_i'\) are opposite to each other. A regular octahedron has one vertex in each of the segments \(P_1P_2,\) \(P_1P_3,\) \(P_1P_4,\) \(P_1'P_2',\) \(P_1'P_3',\) and \(P_1'P_4'.\) What is the octahedron’s side length?

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q19_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
First use the octahedron’s equal edges to determine how far its vertices lie from the two cube corners. Call the vertices on \(P_1P_2,P_1P_3,P_1P_4\) respectively \(U,V,W\), and call those on the corresponding edges from \(P_1'\) respectively \(U',V',W'\). Let the octahedron’s side length be \(s>0\).

Any two of \(U,V,W\) lie on a common cube face. They cannot be opposite octahedron vertices: their midpoint would lie on that cube face, whereas the midpoint of opposite octahedron vertices is the octahedron’s interior center. An interior point of the octahedron cannot lie on the boundary of the cube containing it. Therefore every pair is joined by an octahedron edge, so \(UVW\) is equilateral. The same reasoning applies to \(U'V'W'\).

Write \(a=P_1U\), \(b=P_1V\), and \(c=P_1W\). The three cube edges are perpendicular, so
\[
a^2+b^2=a^2+c^2=b^2+c^2=s^2.
\]
Subtracting these equalities gives \(a=b=c=t\), where \(s^2=2t^2\) and \(0<t\le1\). Applying the same argument at \(P_1'\) shows that \(P_1'U'=P_1'V'=P_1'W'=t\).

Now compare the segments \(UV'\) and \(UW'\). Along the three perpendicular cube-edge directions, \(UV'\) spans distances \(1-t,1-t,1\), while \(UW'\) spans \(1-t,1,1-t\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem twice gives
\[
UV'^2=UW'^2=1+2(1-t)^2.
\]
A vertex of a regular octahedron has only one opposite vertex, so at least one of \(UV'\) and \(UW'\) is an edge. Their common squared length must therefore equal \(s^2\). Hence
\[
2t^2=1+2(1-t)^2=3-4t+2t^2,
\]
which gives \(t=3/4\). This lies within the unit segments, as required. Thus
\[
s=t\sqrt2=\boxed{\frac{3\sqrt2}{4}},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
